blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the principles a tax system is judged against, and read them off a working system.

blocks.heading: The four principles
blocks.text: Adam Smith's principles still frame the judgement. Equity: those with a greater ability to pay bear a larger share. Certainty: the payer knows what is due, when it is due, and how it is to be paid. Convenience: payment falls due where and when it is easy to pay. Economy: the tax costs little to collect relative to what it raises. Each principle is a standard the system is held to, not a description of any one tax.

blocks.heading: The principles in a payslip
blocks.text: Pay-as-you-earn income tax shows three of them at once. A machinist at Oshakati Textiles has income tax taken from each month's wage by the employer and passed to the revenue authority: nothing further is owed later, no journey to a tax office - convenience; the rates and bands were published before the year began - certainty; the employer's payroll collects it with little extra cost - economy. In Japan, salary withholding works the same way, and for the same reasons.

blocks.heading: Where the principles pull apart
blocks.text: A market levy that takes the same N$20 from every trader in Katutura whatever her takings scores well on economy - one collector, one round - and badly on equity, since N$20 from a thin day is a heavier share than from a good one. The principles pull against one another, and a tax system trades among them: simplicity bought at the price of fairness is a choice, not an accident.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The fairness aimed at here returns in topic 4.2 as the redistribution the tax system serves; the households whose wages are taxed are those of topic 3.2.
